5.        Recapitulating the facts, FIR No. 174 of 2021 was

lodged on 04.06.2021 on the basis of the complaint dated

22.04.2021 made by the complainant Devendra Kumar,

alleging an offence against the appellant under Section 7A

of the PC Act, inter alia, that the appellant demanded bribe

in the name of Superintendent of Police. The appellant was

arrested on 01.09.2021. On 08.12.2023, sanction for

prosecution under Section 19 of the PC Act was granted, and

a chargesheet bearing No. 06 of 2024 dated 19.01.2024

came to be filed in respect of the aforesaid offence under the

PC Act against the appellant. On 12.09.2024, the Trial Court

framed a charge against the appellant.


5.1       Adverting to Section 17A of the PC Act at the outset,

it reads as under,

      “17-A. Enquiry or Inquiry or investigation    of
      offences relatable to recommendations made or
      decision taken by public servant in discharge of
      official functions or duties.-

      (1) No police officer shall conduct any enquiry or
      inquiry or investigation into any offence alleged to
      have been committed by a public servant under this
      Act, where the alleged offence is relatable to any
      recommendation made or decision taken by such
      public servant in discharge of his official functions
      or duties, without the previous approval-

             (a) in the case of a person who is or was
             employed, at the time when the offence
             was alleged to have been committed, in
             connection with the affairs of the Union,
             of that Government;

             (b) in the case of a person who is or was
             employed, at the time when the offence
             was alleged to have been committed, in
             connection with the affairs of a State, of
             that Government;

        for cases involving arrest of a person on the spot on
        the charge of accepting or attempting to accept any
        undue advantage for himself or for any other
        person:

        Provided further that the concerned authority shall
        convey its decision under this section within a
        period of three months, which may, for reasons to
        be recorded in writing by such authority, be
        extended by a further period of one month.”



5.1.1      A bare perusal of the aforesaid Section goes to show

that it provides that no police officer shall conduct an

enquiry or investigation into any offence which is alleged to

have been committed by a public servant under the PC Act,

where the alleged offence is relatable to any recommendation

made or decision taken by such public servant, and further that

the same has to be in discharge of official functions or official


Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025             Page 8 of 17
duties of such public servant, against whom enquiry or

investigation is to be initiated.


5.1.2     If those conditions are satisfied, a previous approval of

the competent authority as per sub-clauses (a), (b) and (c) would

be necessary. The First Proviso of the section says that no such

approval shall be necessary in respect of the cases involving

arrest of a person on the spot on the charge of accepting or

attempting to accept any undue advantage for himself or for any

other person. As per the Second Proviso, the authority concerned

shall convey its decision under this provision within stipulated

time, which is extendable by recording reasons for such

extension.


5.2       In Central Bureau of Investigation vs. Santosh

Karnani and Another9, the appellant-Central Bureau of

Investigation was aggrieved by the order of the High Court

of Gujarat whereby the High Court allowed the anticipatory

bail application of the respondent in connection with the FIR

which was in respect of the offence under Section 7 of the

PC Act.




9 (2023) SCC OnLine SC 427




Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025           Page 9 of 17
5.2.1     The     contention       that    the   prior   approval    of

investigation, as per under Section 17A of the PC Act was

not obtained and thus the proceedings initiated against the

respondent were vitiated, was rejected stating that it had no

legal basis,

      “Section 17A merely contemplates that police
      officers shall not conduct any enquiry, inquiry or
      investigation into any offence alleged to have been
      committed by a public servant where the alleged
      offence is relatable to any recommendation made or
      decision taken in discharge of official functions or
      duties, without the previous approval of the
      competent authority. The first proviso to the section
      states that such approval is not necessary in cases
      involving arrest of the person on the spot on the
      charges of accepting undue advantage.”
                                                  (Para 33)


5.2.2     The accusation against the appellant in the

aforementioned case did not involve any recommendation

made or decision taken by him in his official capacity as a

public servant. This Court observed, which observations

equally apply to the facts of the present case.

      “As may be seen, the first proviso to Section 17A
      refers to cases wherein a public servant is charged
      with acceptance of an undue advantage or attempt
      thereof. A prior approval or sanction to investigate
      such an officer in a trap case is likely to defeat the
      very purpose of trap and the investigation, which is
      not the underlying intention of the legislature. The
      investigation against Respondent No. 1, being an
      accused of demanding a bribe, did not require any


Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025             Page 10 of 17
      previous approval of the Central Government. That
      apart, the accusation against Respondent No. 1
      does not revolve around any recommendations
      made or decisions taken by him in his quasi-
      judicial or administrative capacity.”
                                              (Para 34)

5.3       The decision in Santosh Karnani (supra) was

quoted to be relied on in Surendra Dhariwal vs. The State

of Rajasthan and Another Etc. which was Criminal Appeal

Nos. 3717-3718 of 2025 decided on 25.08.2025. Again, it

was a case wherein the FIR was registered for the offence

punishable under Section 7 of the PC Act and Sections 384,

120-B and 201 of the IPC.


5.4       The judicial view on the above score is consistent

and categorical. Yet in another and more recent decision of

this Court in Anil Daima Etc. vs. State of Rajasthan and

Others10, the petitioner before this Court was prosecuted for

the offence punishable under Section 7 and Section 7A

respectively of the PC Act. It was also a case for demand of

illegal gratification as in the present case.


5.4.1     This Court dispelled the contention about the

applicability of Section 17A of the Act, observing,


10 2026 SCC OnLine SC 807




Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025        Page 11 of 17
      “The entire submission of the learned counsel is
      thoroughly misconceived. Section 17-A came to be
      enacted with a particular object. Section 17-A talks
      about enquiry or inquiry or investigation of offences
      relatable to recommendations made or decision
      taken by public servant in discharge of official
      functions or duties. Section 17-A by any stretch of
      imagination cannot be applied to cases of demand
      of illegal gratification.”
                                                   (Para 7)


5.5       In Shankara Bhat vs. State of Kerala and

Others11, the Kerala High Court observed that Section

197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and Section

17A of the PC Act though operate in two different fields and

in distinct situations, they have, in common, the aspect of

offence committed by the public servant while acting or

purporting to act in discharge of his official duty. It was

stated that the commission of crime by public servant which

had no connection with his official duty, cannot be

considered to be falling within the ambit of Section 17A of

the PC Act.


5.5.1     It     was      stated      that       the   offences      like

misappropriation,        falsification     of    accounts,   cheating,

criminal breach of trust, receiving bribes, etc. are beyond


11 2021 SCC OnLine Ker 16357




Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025               Page 12 of 17
the scope of the provision. The same dictum of law was

reiterated by the same High Court in M.R. Simon vs. State

of Kerala12.


6.        An unequivocal position of law emanates from the

above decisions about the scope and extent of applicability

of Section 17A of the PC Act which contemplates taking a

prior approval before investigation or inquiry against a

public servant. The language of the provision itself outlines

and circumscribes the ambit of operation of the provision.

The decisive phrase in the section is “discharge his official

functions or duties”. Though the legislature has intended to

protect the public servant from being prosecuted by

engrafting Section 17A in the statute book, the protection

envisaged could be extended only if the conditions

contemplated in the Section are satisfied. The Section

cannot be viewed to have an omnibus application.


6.1       In order that the provisions of Section 17A of the PC

Act    applies,      there     has     to    be   a   “decision”    or

“recommendation” by a public servant against whom an


12 2024 SCC OnLine Ker 7255




Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025            Page 13 of 17
enquiry or investigation is to be initiated. Such “decision” or

“recommendation”          shall     be    a      “decision”    taken     or

“recommendation”          made     by    such      public     servant    in

discharge of his official functions or duties. In other words,

the alleged offence against the public servant must be

relatable to any recommendation made or decision taken by

such public servant in discharge of his official duties. These

primary and essential aspects are absent in the present case

to attract Section 17A of the PC Act. The allegation is of

demanding illegal gratification by the appellant, which is a

pure criminal act unconnected to discharge of the official

functions or duties.


6.2       Thus, from the plain language of the provision of

Section 17A, it is evident that the provision is confined to be

applied in the situations where there is a recommendation

or a decision taken by a public servant in discharge of his

official duties. The allegation against the appellant in the

present case is that of a criminal act, namely that the

appellant demanded illegal gratification of Rs.1.5 lakh. The

conduct on the part of the appellant, by no stretch of

imagination, can be treated as part of the discharge of his

Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025                 Page 14 of 17
official functions. It was not in any way relatable to

recommendation or a decision taken by the appellant in

discharge of his official duties but was an act unrelated to

his official duty.


6.3       In the aforesaid view, Section 17A of the PC Act is

not applicable in the case of appellant herein. None of the

ingredients provided for in the Section is satisfied to attract

its operation. The act of demanding a bribe is a pure

criminal act, not connected with official functions and not

relatable to or having any linkage with recommendation or

decision of the appellant in his capacity, as public servant.

In the facts and circumstances of the case, therefore, the act

of the appellant does not fall within the protective umbrella

of Section 17A of the Act. It could not be said that the

proceedings were vitiated for want of sanction.


7.        Disposing of the submission of the learned counsel

for the appellant that the issue regarding the validity of

Section 17A of the PC Act is referred to a larger bench by

this Court as per order dated 13.01.2026 passed in Centre

for Public Interest Litigation (supra), it is to be stated that



Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025      Page 15 of 17
the reference has no connection with the issue involved in

the present case since the present case could be decided

without awaiting the reference, when Section 17A of the PC

Act has no applicability at all.


8.        In the impugned judgment and order, the High

Court has noted that subsequent sanction for prosecution

under Section 19 of the PC Act has been taken. A faint

attempt was made on behalf of the appellant to contend that

it was a belated sanction obtained. Evaluating the said

aspect in the light of the operative facts in the present case,

firstly as held above, Section 17A has no application. As far

as Section 19 is concerned, sanction was taken as alleged

before the cognizance was taken, it would amount to mere

an irregularity. It cannot be said to be vitiating the entire

criminal proceedings and the trial that would take place, on

the count of said aspect as well. The trial would be

conducted on its merits, where the respective parties would

raise their rival contentions.


9.        The High Court was justified in dismissing the

Criminal Revision Petition of the appellant. The judgment



Criminal Appeal @ SLP (Crl.) No. 11709 of 2025      Page 16 of 17
and order of the High Court warrants no interference. It is

upheld.


10.       For the reasons recorded by the High Court and for

those supplied additionally in this judgment by this Court,

it is ruled that Section 17A of the PC Act would not be

attracted in the facts of the case and that want of prior

sanction thereunder by the competent authority, has in no

manner vitiated the initiation of criminal proceedings

against the appellant.


11.       The appeal stands dismissed.

11.     Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank Limited, the Appellant in Civil Appeal Nos.

13630 and 13631 of 2026, filed Writ Petition No. 8661 of 2020 challenging

the Order dated 26.12.2019 passed by the CLA. The impugned Order




                                         8
dismissed the Writ Petition. The summary of the conclusions is stated

hereunder: -


A.    The High Court adopted the factual and legal conclusions recorded in

paragraph 15 of the Commissioner of Land Administration Order dated

26.12.2019, which characterise the 2011 DRO, Tiruvallur grant of patta as a

product of administrative fraud.

B.    The land was classified as "Kanakkankuttai" before and throughout the

settlement proceedings under the Act, 1948. Communal water bodies vest in

the State free from all encumbrances and cannot be granted on patta to either

ryots or erstwhile landholders.

C.    Section 14-A of the Act, 1948 expressly bars the grant of patta even in

respect of private tanks or ooranis and mandates the cancellation of any patta

erroneously or mistakenly issued over such lands. The DRO, Tiruvallur, had

no authority to reclassify communal poramboke land into ryoti land. The

power of reclassification under Section 20-A of the Tamil Nadu Estates Land

Act, 1908, was extinguished upon its repeal by the Act, 1948.

D.    That G.O.Ms. No. 1300 dated 30.04.1971 applied strictly to ryoti lands

in continuous occupation and could never authorise regularisation or grant

of patta for water bodies.

E.    That Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank is a mere mortgagee claiming under

P. Ramadoss. Because P. Ramadoss procured the patta by fraud over

Government watercourse land, the mortgage created no valid charge against

the State. Since the Bank’s mortgagor had no marketable title, hearing the

Bank would have been an empty formality that could not alter the legal

character of a public water body.

F.    The Court directed the District Administration to evict all occupants,

demolish all unauthorised residential and commercial structures across the

entire 1.68 acres of Survey No. 572, and restore the water body within 16

weeks.

G.    The Court ordered the District Collector, Tiruvallur, to inquire into the

fraudulent issuance of the 2011 Patta, initiate disciplinary and criminal

proceedings against all responsible officials, bar them from key posts, and

place them under surveillance by the Vigilance and Anti-Corruption

Department.

H.    The Court dismissed the Writ Petition while preserving the Bank’s

statutory liberty to proceed against the borrower/mortgagor under SARFAESI

from limitation under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002.

12.   Accordingly, the flat owner and Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank Limited

have filed Civil Appeal Nos. 13629-13631 of 2026, challenging the impugned

Order.

13.   We have heard Mr. T. Raja, learned Senior Counsel and Mr K.S.

Mahadevan,     learned   Counsel    for    the   Appellants   and   Ms.   Jayasree

Narasimhan, Counsel for the Respondents.

14.   Counsel for the Appellants argue that the impugned Order assumes

that the subject matter of the Civil Appeals is a tank. This finding is baseless,

and the existence of the tank is recorded by reference to an Order passed by



                                          10
the High Court in Writ Petition No. 10075 of 2018. According to him, the Court

made no such finding in that Writ Petition. The Chennai Metropolitan

Authority has shown the subject land as a “Mixed Residential Zone”. The zonal

development plan conclusively proves that the subject land is ryotwari land

and not a water body. The DRO, Tiruvallur, is competent under G.O.Ms.

No.1300 dated 30.04.1971 read with G.O.Ms. No.370 dated 03.10.1974, to

entertain a petition for the grant of Ryotwari patta. The Commissioner of Land

Administration did not hear the bank, the flat owners, or any bona fide

purchasers of land. Section 14-A of the Act, 1948, is not attracted to the

circumstances of the case.


15.   Advocate Jayasree Narasimhan argues that the earliest resurvey and

settlement record of 1911 described the subject matter as “Government

Poramboke – Kanakkam Kuttai”. The Registered Deed inter se parties does not

affect the rights possessed under the Act, 1948, by the Government/Local

Bodies. The DRO, Tiruvallur, exercised jurisdiction not available to him.

Without prejudice to the first contention, it is argued that the DRO, Tiruvallur,

acted beyond the record. The survey and settlement operations, concluded

long ago by the grant of ryotwari pattas, were followed by renewed efforts as

late as 2010 to secure a ryotwari patta with urbanisation. The Revenue Officer

does not have jurisdiction to grant a patta for non-ryoti land, i.e., communal

land, Government Poramboke, bank, forest, etc. After examining the record,

the CLA rightly set aside the patta dated 21.01.2011. The Assignee/P.

Ramadoss did not challenge the CLA Order dated 26.12.2019, but as

Mortgagee, Tamil Nadu Mercantile Bank Limited questioned it in Writ Petition


                                       11
No. 8661 of 2020. The impugned Order rejected the challenge for valid and

available reasons. To protect non-ryoti land from being granted as ryotwari

pattas, the State Legislature enacted Section 14-A of the Act, 1948, and

nullified pattas granted prior to the amendment for private land or oorani.

Section 14-A further deems that, for private land or oorani, the landholder or

any other person is entitled to a ryotwari patta under the Act, 1948. Therefore,

the Government's development work is for the restoration of a water body,

and no exception can be made.


16.   We have perused the record, including the latest Report dated

09.10.2026, filed by the District Collector, Tiruvallur. The said Report is made

part of this Judgment.

17.   The Appellant takes exception to the Order dated 26.12.2019 on the

ground that no Authority has adjudicated that the subject matter of the

Appeal is a tank. In our considered view, this contention appears untenable

because the Act, 1948 does not require adjudication to protect communal

Government Poramboke, etc. Simply put, the Ryotiwari tenures under the Act,

1948 apply to Ryoti land covered by the said Act. The inquiry in this behalf

determines the nature of the land, the type of enjoyment, the period of

enjoyment, and the entitlement to grant of patta.

18.   In Salem Municipality v. P. Kumar and Others,3 this Court considered

the definitions under Sections 3(15), 3(16) and 14-A(1) of the Act, 1948. The

background in the Judgment concerns a tank and tank bund. Between 1940

and 1946, Zamindar Ganambal granted multiple seasonal 8-month leases

(November–June) for the “Chinneri Tank Bund” dry wasteland to S.

Vijayaranga Mudaliar, who held possession before the July monsoon

submergence. Following the Act, 1948, the land vested in the State, and the

Government took possession on 12.01.1951. Despite Mudaliar's eligibility for

a Ryotwari Patta under Section 11 of the Act, 1948, the plaintiff, P.C.

Pachiappan, purchased the 4.91-acre suit property on 29.09.1952. The

Plaintiff's Applications for a Ryotwari Patta were rejected because the land

constitutes "Achuvan Eri", i.e., a Class IV irrigation lake, and must be

preserved as a submergible tank for local farmers (ayacutdars). On

23.02.1984, the State Government transferred the entire 24.62-acre area to

the Salem Municipality for a new bus stand. In response, the Plaintiff filed

three successive Suits for declaration of title and injunctions, culminating in

the High Court, where the judgment of the First Appellate Court was set aside.

In the above factual background, the following paragraphs are excerpted:

18.1 Finally, it was held that the Revenue entries show that the entire area

of 24.62 acres had been recorded as a tank continuously from 1950 to 1995.

Since the land formed part of a tank reserved for common use, no right

accrued to the plaintiff to claim Ryotwari Patta, as his predecessor was not a

Ryot and the disputed land was not Ryotwari land. The vendor did not hold

the land for 12 consecutive years, so no right, title, or interest accrued to the

Vendor or the Plaintiff.

19.   Therefore, non-Ryoti lands do not fall within the scope of granting a

patta under the Act, 1948. Whenever a dispute arises over entitlement to a

patta, the nature of the land is determined by appreciating entries in the

earliest Revenue Records, including Survey and Settlement Records. The

Appellants do not contend that the Revenue Records show the subject matter

as Ryoti land during the Survey and Settlement operation or the

contemporaneous faslis. Since the Appellants claim a Ryotwari patta, they

must establish the ingredients for the land to be termed Ryoti land and that

P. Ramadoss is entitled to a Ryotwari Patta. Accordingly, the first objection to

the impugned Orders is rejected.

20.   It is argued that, under the Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning

Act, 1971 (“Act, 1971”), the urban area development plan for the land has

been notified as a “Mixed Residential Zone”. Therefore, the basis of the


                                            14
Commissioner's Order or the Writ Court’s Order is completely effaced, and

consequently the cancellation of the Ryotwari Patta vide Order dated

26.04.2019 is illegal.

21.   The Statement of Objects and Scope of the Acts of 1971 and 1948 is

noted. Therefore, notifying a block of area in the development zone as

commercial, industrial, residential, or mixed residential/mixed-use cannot be

construed as taking away the Government's rights in Poramboke lands,

forests, water bodies/tanks, etc. The said argument does not take into

account that zoning regulations are not confined to a single survey number

but apply when an individual undertakes development activity in the notified

area. The development of a plot conforms to the notified zoning requirement.

Reference to the subject matter being in a mixed residential zone, either in

fact or in law, cannot be treated as effacing the effect of Section 14-A of the

Act, 1948.

22.   It is further argued that the CLA did not hear the Mortgagee and the

flat owners while setting aside the Ryotwari Patta. This argument requires

examining whether the CLA heard no one or only the person interested in the

subject matter when passing the Order dated 26.12.2019. The Appellants

claim that P. Ramadoss, who continues to hold an interest in the balance

extent of the subject matter, was heard, and that the flat buyers were not

heard during the pendency of the proceedings before the CLA. The objection

on the ground of denial of opportunity is not available to the Appellants

because the Notice was issued to the person who had the Ryotwari Patta in

his favour and claimed an interest in the property.



                                      15
23.     It is argued that the Revenue Records do not record the subject matter

as a water body but instead record it in the names of private individuals. This

argument is far removed from the Revenue extracts on which the CLA passed

the Order dated 26.12.2019. The record filed by the State reinforces that the

subject matter has been classified as a tank/Government Poramboke in the

Revenue Records from the earliest point in time. This ground is equally

untenable and warrants rejection.

24.     Section 14-A of the Act, 1948, prohibits officers from considering and

granting Ryotwari Patta for non-Ryoti land. The Legislature designed a

prohibitory mechanism to prevent changes in land classification. The said

Section even renders the Order already issued void. That being the statutory

scheme, the DRO, Tiruvallur, without any reason, went beyond the provisions

of the said Act and granted Patta.

25.     The above consideration records findings on the Appellants' entitlement

to any relief in the Civil Appeals in relation to the subject matter. Other

circumstances in the matter include the grant of Permit No. C 3031 on

24.05.2005 by the Avadi Municipality for establishing the timber mart; the

revenue department changed the Town Survey Land Register and approved

the subdivision of the subject matter; the Avadi Municipality approved the

building plans for the construction of apartments; and, as per the Report

dated 09.10.2026 of the District Collector, Tiruvallur, the present existence of

apartments is to an extent of 0.22 acres. The impugned Judgment directed

the demolition of the existing structures and the restoration of the water

body.



                                       16
26.   In the present case, the Municipal Administration has approved and

sanctioned the building plans. The Revenue, without realising its obligation

under Section 14-A of the Act, 1948, is changing the nature in the Town

Survey Land Records. These permissions/Orders lead a bona fide purchaser

to believe that the subject matter is available and free from any objectionable

use. The Court is constrained to observe that a bona fide purchaser for

consideration looks at the presumptive value of entries and town survey

records while purchasing the property. At the government's convenience, the

nature of the land is changed. The remedies against the developer and the

landowner are independent, but the State and its officers ought not to be

allowed to pass on without paying the price for such willy-nilly felicitation by

the officers of the State.

27.   Because of these Orders and Revenue Records, the flat owners have

been led to believe that the Government has no interest under Section 14-A

of the Act, 1948. Therefore, directing the demolition of flats without examining

the hardship of the flat owners and the independent remedies available to

them in law against the owner of the land and the developer of the apartments

would cause irreparable financial injury and throw the families on the streets.

In the circumstances of the case, to ameliorate the possible hardship and,

without committing a breach of Section 14-A of the Act, 1948, we direct the

Chief Secretary, State of Tamil Nadu, and the District Collector, Tiruvallur, to

allot a vacant, commensurate site to the owners of the flats represented by

the Society, preferably within 6 months from today, and thereafter to

undertake the demolition of the constructed area to an extent of 0.22 acres.



                                      17
28.   Subject to the above direction, we see no reason to interfere with the

impugned Judgment. The development work in the vacant and unoccupied

area may be completed expeditiously without hindrance. The flat owners and

the Appellant Bank are free to avail themselves of the remedies in law against

the developer/Owner/Mortgagor, as the case may be, before the Competent

Civil Court. The State Government is free to initiate or conclude disciplinary

action against the erring Officers for failing to maintain the records and water

bodies.

29.   For the above consideration and reasons, the Civil Appeals are

dismissed. No order as to costs.

      ANALYSIS

      NATURE OF TEMPLE PROPERTY AND THE STATE’S ROLE
      AS CUSTODIAN

23.   Before turning to the rival contentions, it is useful to recall why

      property belonging to religious institutions is treated differently

      from ordinary property. Our country’s religious institutions are

      not merely places of worship, they are, in law and, in fact,

      repositories of considerable wealth, land, buildings, jewellery

      and specie, accumulated over centuries through the offerings of

      ordinary devotees and the endowments of kings and commoners

      alike, given in the faith that what was dedicated to the deity

      would remain dedicated to the deity in perpetuity. That wealth,

      once given, ceases to belong to the donor, to the priest, to the



                                Page 14 of 31
           trustee, or to the State; it vests in the deity, and every hand

           through which it subsequently passes holds it only in trust for

           the deity and, through the deity, for the community of

           worshippers it was meant to serve. Every custodian holds it only

           in trust for the deity and the worshippers it serves.


24.        A seven-Judge Bench of this Court in Commissioner, Hindu

           Religious    Endowments,       Madras    v.   Sri   Lakshmindra

           Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt4, held that while Articles

           25 and 26 of the Constitution protect religious belief and

           practice, they do not immunise the secular and economic

           administration of religious property from regulation by law. The

           same view was reaffirmed in A.S. Narayana Deekshitulu v.

           State of Andhra Pradesh5, where the administration of temple

           funds and offices was held to be a secular function distinct from

           the freedom of worship itself.

highest bid cannot be a reason to discard the highest bid.” 2026 SCC OnLine 24, para 32.

22.   We are, therefore, not in agreement with the reasoning drawn

by the High Court, and the judgment and order of the High Court, to

that extent, are set aside.

23.   However, the story does not end here.

24.   In our opinion, the difficulty arose because of the reason that

the High Court, instead of either dismissing the writ petition at the

admission stage itself or granting an interim order staying the

cancellation letters dated 27.01.2023 and 09.02.2023, proceeded to

permit the Chandigarh Administration to hold a fresh E-Auction.

That interim arrangement made by the High Court, has opened up

a second phase of litigation which has continued for more than two

years. Surprisingly, when the High Court took up the writ petition for

final hearing, it did not consider the consequences of the rights and

liabilities of parties that had been created due to the subsequent

auction. High Court simply proceeded to consider the writ petition

on its merits and disposed it of. In the order impugned before us, the

High Court has not discussed the consequences of the interim order

directing the conduct of a fresh E-Auction and the status report

submitted by the Chandigarh Administration after the successful

conclusion of the re-auction.

25.   The subsequent auction that was conducted is legal and valid.

In fact, the said auction was conducted pursuant to the direction of

                                Page 16 of 18
the High Court on 10.02.2023, wherein even M/s Bedi Hospital was

permitted to participate. Having conducted and concluded a fresh

auction, the Chandigarh Administration placed a status report

before the High Court indicating clearly that the subsequent e-

auction fetched an additional amount of Rs. 6 Crores. Six crores is

not a small amount, and this Court cannot shut its eyes to the glaring

reality of the facts that have unfolded about price discovery.

26.   Faced with this reality, we inquired with Mr. Patwalia, learned

senior counsel, if his client would be willing to match the price

offered by the appellant. With some amount of hesitation, but after

consulting his client, we were informed M/s Bedi Hospital would be

willing to match the bid amount of the appellant and pay Rs. 18.30

crores as the final price for Site No. 4. On the other hand, Mr. Guru

Krishna Kumar, learned senior counsel for the appellant, submitted

that his client paid the entire consideration and that it would be

unjust to permit M/s Bedi Hospital to replace him by matching the

price, particularly when the earlier amount deposited was refunded,

and M/s Bedi Hospital chose not to take part in the subsequent

auction.

27.   Having considered the matter in detail and having reflected on

the unfortunate situation that has been created due to the

inconclusive interim arrangement made by the High Court, we are

                              Page 17 of 18
of the opinion that interests of justice and public purpose will be

subserved if we direct the Chandigarh Administration to conduct a

fresh e-auction of Site No. 4 after following the due procedure.

28.   For the reasons stated above, the present set of civil appeals

is allowed, and the judgment and order of the High Court dated

01.04.2025 is set aside. The Chandigarh Administration is directed

to hold a fresh e-auction for Site No. 4 in Sector 33C, Chandigarh,

by following the procedure prescribed under the Chandigarh Estate

Rules, 2007. The entire process should commence and conclude

within a period of 3 months from today.

    some submissions concerning the merits of the matter. However, it is

    prayer for bail. Thus, while on the one hand, it would not be entirely

    correct to claim that the appellant was wholly unrepresented before

    winter vacation particularly when such petition had not been made

    returnable on a specific date falling during such vacation or the Single

    Judge had not directed its listing before the Vacation Bench. To have

    obtained listing of a petition, without adequate notice to the appellant,

    was clearly an attempt to steal a march by even misleading the Court.



                                     9
28. Had it been a case of arrest for a heinous offence, we would have taken

    a very strict view of the respondent’s conduct.

29. Be that as it may, regard being had to the entire turn of events, we

    are of the view that though the bail granted by the High Court to the

    respondent may not be set aside at this stage, certainly the matter

    needs to be remitted to the Single Judge who had the occasion to deal

    with the criminal petition on 26th December, 2025 for its fresh

    consideration.

30. Thus, we set aside that part of the impugned order whereby the

    criminal petition stood disposed of with the result that the same shall

    revive on the file of the High Court; and we direct that instead of the

    bail granted by the Single Judge, the respondent shall continue to

    remain on interim bail on earlier terms and conditions. Appellant is

    granted liberty to place all materials on record by filing a counter

    affidavit within two weeks, peremptorily. Respondent will have a

    week’s time to file his rejoinder. The Single Judge shall, thereafter,

    decide the criminal petition on its own merits, preferably by the end of

    this year. Needless to observe, interim bail granted to the respondent

    shall be operative till such time further orders are passed by the Single

    Judge on the criminal petition.

31. The appeal stands disposed of on the above terms.

32. Pending applications, if any, shall stand closed.




                                      10
33. Before parting, we wish to make certain observations on urgent listing

    of matters, be it a petition or application or appeal, before a Bench of

    a high court when the court is on vacation.

34. In cases of the present nature, where a Bench of a high court directs

    listing of a petition “two weeks hence” and the day following expiry of

    the period of “two weeks”, in terms of such direction, happens to fall

    in the midst of a vacation, the period of two weeks should ordinarily

    be computed by the registry of each such court excluding the period

    during which the court is on vacation. However, if the petition is made

    returnable on a specific date by the Bench which falls during the

    vacation or the Bench directs listing before the Vacation Bench, such

    petition should ideally be accordingly listed. This, of course, would be

    subject to the relevant rules framed by the high courts.

35. These observations, aimed at serving the interest of justice better, are

    essential to secure uniformity as well as to ensure that litigants are

    not prejudiced due to an inadvertent act of the court.

      be allowed to be pursued further, we refrain from noting the

      submissions of Mr. Nuli on the merits of the complaint itself.

10.   Section 125-A of the RoP Act reads as follows:

        125-A. Penalty for filing false affidavit, etc.—A candidate who
        himself or through his proposer, with intent to be elected in an
        election,—
        (i) fails to furnish information relating to sub-section (1) of Section
        33-A; or
        (ii) gives false information which he knows or has reason to believe
        to be false; or
        (iii) conceals any information,
        in his nomination paper delivered under sub-section (1) of Section
        33 or in his affidavit which is required to be delivered under sub-
        section (2) of Section 33-A, as the case may be, shall

                                                             (emphasis ours)

11.   It is significant to note that sub-clauses (i) to (iii) of clause (a) of

      sub-section (1) of Section 195(1) of the Cr. PC impose a statutory

      prohibition on a court in relation to taking cognisance of offences

      punishable under Sections 172 to 188, IPC or of abetment

      of/attempt to/criminal conspiracy to commit such offences, except

      on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of

      some other public servant to whom he is administratively

      subordinate. It is plain that the text of clause (a) of sub-section

      (1) of Section 195 does not include Section 125-A of the RoP Act.

      Should we read into Section 195, Cr. PC a prohibition in respect

      of Section 125-A of the RoP Act also, apart from those expressly

      included? If indeed it were the intention of the legislature that

      cognizance of any offence relating to furnishing of false

      information by a candidate in an affidavit with intent of being

      elected in an election (referred to in Section 125-A of the RoP Act)

      could only be taken if the complainant were a public servant, the

      same could have been provided by an amendment of Section 195,

      Cr. PC since Section 125-A of the RoP Act is of fairly recent origin.

      Significantly, Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act with effect

      from 24th August, 2002, while it is noticed that Section 195,

      Cr. PC suffered an amendment thereafter in April, 2006. The

      legislature is presumed to be conscious of its insertion of Section

      125-A in the RoP Act four years back. It stands to reason that

      omission of the legislature to include Section 125-A of the RoP Act

                               Page 7 of 9
      in Section 195, Cr. PC is deliberate and no court, in terms of the

      latter provision, would be barred from taking cognizance of an

      alleged offence under Section 125-A of the RoP Act, even on the

      complaint lodged by a private person. This interpretation is also

      fortified by the absence of any provision in any enactment

      stipulating that a complaint in relation to an offence under Section

      125-A of the RoP Act can only be lodged by a public servant as

      well as the ordainment in Section 125-A that the penalty it

      envisages is “notwithstanding anything contained in any other law

      for the time being in force”. This means that the rigour of Section

      195, Cr. PC would not be applicable insofar as a complaint lodged

      by a private person, alleging an offence under Section 125-A of

      the RoP Act, under Section 200, Cr. PC, is concerned, whereby the

      court is urged to penalise the offender for furnishing false

      information in an affidavit to get elected. The High Court was,

      therefore, clearly in error in returning the finding that it did.

12.   Having so held on a plain construction of the statutory provisions,

      we need not fall back on the clarifications provided by the ECI.

      Even though the ECI is supreme in its own sphere and has,

      indeed, issued guidelines/press notes based on its understanding

      of the statutory provisions, interpretation of statutes is primarily

      the task of the courts and such guidelines/press notes do not bind

      us.

13.    In conclusion, we hold that a private complaint alleging offence

       committed under Section 125-A, RoP Act need not pass muster of

       the rigours of Section 195, Cr. PC, as held by the High Court. If at

       all a complaint is lodged to harass an elected candidate or

       frivolous allegations are levelled therein, the laws of the country

       duly equip and empower the competent magistrates to pass such

       order(s) as they deem fit and proper commensurate with the facts

       and circumstances of each case.

14.    Having answered the question, we reiterate that the decision of

       the High Court closing the proceedings before the trial magistrate

       stands upheld for reasons different from the one assigned by it.

15.    On the above terms, the appeal stands disposed of.

16.    Parties shall bear their own costs.

36. Before we embark upon our discussion and reasoning, we

37. The law of limitation, as a procedural law, finds its roots in the
     maxims “interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium” which means
     that it is in the interest of the State that there should be a limit
     to litigation and “vigilantibus non dormientibus jura
     subveniunt” - the law assists the vigilant and not those who
     sleep over their rights. It specifies that a litigant ought to be
     diligent, careful and proactive in enforcing and protecting his
     rights for a purpose that the litigation ought to be raised before
     the cause expires and also to prevent the litigation from being
     dragged for a prolonged period of time. It cannot be construed
     that the period of limitation bars the court from enforcing
     substantive justice. As the scope of the Act specifies, it is to
     make sure that the parties knock the doors of the court within
     a time bound manner so as to not render their cause otiose. A
     substantial cause seeking justice has a lifespan and once the
     cause dies, it cannot be revived by dilatory tactics by clinging
     to another cause. Thus, the period of limitation cannot be
     extended by any party to make it naturally convenient to bring
     the cause within the period of limitation.

24.    The history of Letters Patent informs us that the establishment

of the High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras was necessitated

on account of uncertainty in the judicial administration during the East

India Company regime in India. The Regulating Act of 1773 empowered

the Crown by Charter to erect and establish a Supreme Court at Fort

William with full power and charge to exercise and perform all civil,

criminal, admiralty and ecclesiastical jurisdictions in the Presidency

towns. On 26th March 1774, a Charter was issued by King George III

establishing a Court of Record, the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort

William in Bengal. Later, the Supreme Courts at Madras and Bombay

were established by King George II. Under the Government of India Act,

1858, all territories in India came to be governed directly by and in the

name of the Crown. Then came the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (24-

25 Victoriae Reginae) which was passed on 6th August 1861 declaring it

lawful for Her Majesty, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of United

Kingdom, to erect and establish a High Court of Judicature at Fort

William in Bengal and by like Letters Patent to erect and establish like

High Courts at Madras and Bombay. Under the Indian High Courts Act,

1861, it was provided under 9th Section that each of the High Courts

shall have and exercise, original as well as appellate, all such civil,

criminal, admiralty, vice-admiralty, testamentary, interstate and

matrimonial jurisdiction in the Presidency for which it was established.

It was further provided that the High Courts shall exercise all such

powers and authority for and in relation to the administration of justice

in the Presidency for which it was established as Her Majesty may by

such Letters Patent grant and direct, subject to limitations as may be

prescribed. Under 10th Section, it was provided that all jurisdictions

exercised by the Supreme Courts of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay over

the inhabitants of such parts of India shall be exercised by such High

Courts until the Crown otherwise provides.

28.      However, the jurisdiction of the Letters Patent Bench to interfere

with the concurrent findings of fact should not be understood as if the

Letters Patent Bench can interfere in every matter because it is

exercising the powers of the appellate Court. The jurisdiction of the

Letters Patent Bench to examine a question of fact is not without fetters.

The Letters Patent Bench can be justified in reopening a question of fact

if it necessarily touches upon the merits of the case and is likely to have

a bearing on the decision in the case. It may be argued that the Letters

Patent Bench of the High Court is entitled to review findings of fact. But

what is necessary to keep in mind is that there is an inherent limitation

on exercise of powers by the appellate Bench. This is one of the well

settled legal principles that the appellate Court should not interfere with

the judgment of the Court of first instance unless a clear mistake which

will change the outcome of the case is found to have been committed by

the Court. The Letters Patent Bench should ordinarily be slow and

refrain from interfering with the discretion exercised by the writ Court

under Article 226 of the Constitution. A Letters Patent Bench sitting as

a Court of Correction exercises the same jurisdiction as is vested in the
                                                                             Page 25 of 27
Single Judge but the Letters Patent Bench is required to give due weight

to the decision of the writ Court where it has exercised its discretion on

relevant considerations.


29.    There may be different situations and the aggrieved party may

raise a host of grounds before the Letters Patent Bench. Some of the

grounds may be based on a question of law and the other may be just a

question of fact. The aggrieved party may also raise issues pertaining to

appreciation of evidence. But the Letters Patent Bench can interfere in

the matter only where the findings are demonstrably erroneous and the

mistake is glaring on the face of record. There must exist cogent grounds

and such grounds are not projected on some minor mistake in the

judgment under challenge. The Letters Patent Bench is not entitled to

interfere with the decision of writ Court on mere showing of some error

of fact or in law. If the decision rendered by the writ Court in exercise of

the powers under Article 226 of the Constitution is in furtherance of

justice, equity and good conscience and is not against public policy then

the Letters Patent Bench constituted under Clause 15 of the Letters

Patent of Madras High Court or similar provisions of the Letters Patent

of other High Courts cannot exercise its appellate jurisdiction under the

Letters Patent to interfere with the writ Court’s decision. Simply put, the

Letters Patent Bench can not interfere with the decision rendered by the

writ Court which is otherwise just and reasonable.
